  "summary": "S1 — Fact: deliver a small, single-player Battleship game usable by the requester in a browser against a computer opponent. S2 — Fact: use Node.js for the server and include tests. Boundaries — Fact: the repository is empty, this intake has no tools or files, and this stage implements nothing; the browser is the named delivery target, granting delivery to that target, with no named hosted deployment or external account. Assumption: a locally started server and browser are sufficient; hosted release, multiplayer, accounts, and persistence are outside the recorded scope. Visibility — The isolated run's source checkout stays at its snapshot until final return; the game becomes usable in the browser after the delivered server is started. Any deployed target would show an outcome only after release. Interaction and state — Recorded defaults: one anonymous player is identified by the current browser session, with no account or cross-person, cross-device, or cross-session sharing; game state lasts until reload, which ends it; the computer's unhit ship positions stay hidden from the player until revealed by play. Rules — Recorded default: use standard alternating Battleship turns, reject illegal or repeated shots, and end when a fleet is destroyed; discovery must settle remaining rule details before implementation and rule checks. Discovery first establishes available browser-testing capabilities, then chooses how to verify a complete game at the browser boundary; this blocks completion of that check. The recorded local-delivery default needs no external access; any requirement for a hosted destination would need a person to identify and authorize that destination before release, but does not block local delivery.
